touches.text: More than one builder runs at a time, so work is kept apart by branches: each ticket's work on its own branch, named by the ticket id, merged locally with git, no pull request (GitHub is hosting only). WHY: "the best way to manage scaling is branches."

A row number is the same on every box. Storing a memory first reserves its slot from the librarian on the home box (CAIRN_HOME_HOST, 6.3.7.4), so two boxes are never handed the same slot, and the slot stays reserved until the write is complete. If a box's list is shorter than the slot (eg it holds rows up to 100 and is handed 123 while a sync is bringing the rest), it adds the open slots in between as blanks, and the sync fills them in as it proceeds. WHY: node ids are in every link and blob pointer, so a row has to mean the same node everywhere.

One bus per cairn instance, not per host. Each box runs its own bus, and the buses talk to one another, so a device always talks to the bus on its own box; together they are the instance's one bus. A device runs on one box; the other boxes reach it over the buses. No box needs a full set of devices. WHY: so the instance can run several heavy tasks at once across boxes.

The sleep token goes round in sequence, one sleeper at a time, so no one sleeper takes the whole system to everyone else's cost. The order itself doesn't matter: alphabetical by device, then by instance, the same on every box and nothing stored.

One setup question: "Is this a cairn home? No? Then what's the hostname/IP for the cairn home I should attach to?" The answer is an env var (CAIRN_HOME_HOST), beside the ones for where the repo and the runtime folder are.

Prebuild face: the chart chain, eight machines, each answering one question before a build begins: orient (what is asked, where does it live), constrain (what bounds it), survey (what already exists), decompose (how does it split), triage (what first, by what standard), hypothesize (what do we expect, how would we know we're wrong), validate (what does DONE mean, measured), and after the build, verdict (what done actually meant).
Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).
Hollow runs: proves a proof goes red when the build is removed.

Seals: one current validation per proof, beside the proof. A seal holds while the code it measured is unchanged. [Q#90: A proof's seal is one record, so the newest OS to seal replaces the other's, and a proof with teeth for both OSes reds on every single OS. Measured 2026-11-12: a Windows reseal of a mixed proof overwrote the Linux seal. Do seals go per OS (validations/<os>/, or an OS key in the record), or is one OS the sealing box?]
A timed-out run is its own outcome, not red.
rehearsal: the cheapest model reads a ticket cold and tries to build it on paper, saying where it got stopped or what is missing.

The chart chain machines (9.3.2): orient, constrain, survey, decompose, triage, hypothesize, validate, verdict. [Q#98: The verdict's instrument run, and the proofs that exercise it, need bubblewrap, which Windows does not have, so `cairn test --exec` refuses there ("the instance seal is not confirmed ... bubblewrap (bwrap) is not installed") and three teeth stay red on Windows: test_the_instrument_is_run (two teeth) and the standing-verdict-proofs-stay-green check. Measured 2026-11-13. Whether Windows gets its own seal is the per-OS seal question in Q#90 (9.4.2.3.3); this one is the narrow choice that stands beside it: until that is settled, do the bwrap teeth skip on Windows (and read as not-run there), or do they stay red until Windows has a seal of its own?]
orient: the measuring scans before a build (where is X called, what's in each component). WHY: a build starts from what is, measured, not recalled. USERS: CodeMother's orient machine.
scratch: a proof's throwaway temp dirs and worktrees, cleaned up by the door. WHY: a run must leave nothing behind (4.3.1.7). USERS: the tester.
